profile.campus: AWS Northern Virginia (Data Center Alley) -- US-EAST-1 region, Loudoun / Prince William / Fairfax counties
profile.reading:
This building is one of the data center structures Amazon Web Services operates in Northern Virginia, within the corridor of eastern Loudoun, Prince William, and Fairfax counties that the data center industry calls Data Center Alley, described in trade press as the largest concentration of data centers in the world. AWS traces its Virginia data center presence back to 2006, making this one of the company's original hyperscale cloud regions, now designated US-EAST-1. The corridor grew up around the MAE-East internet exchange point that formed near Tysons and Ashburn in the 1990s, which drew network carriers and later cloud and colocation operators to locate near dense fiber connectivity.

AWS's own public affairs materials, published on aboutamazon.com, state that the company invested $51.9 billion in capital and operating expenses on its Virginia data center infrastructure between 2011 and 2021, and in January 2023 announced a further $35 billion committed to build additional data center campuses across Virginia through 2040. AWS reports its Virginia operations generated $8.2 billion in regional GDP over 2011 to 2021, supported an average of 7,340 full time equivalent jobs at local businesses across that period, and employed 8,710 people directly in the state by 2021, a figure AWS later put at more than 8,800. In 2022, AWS paid $334 million in Virginia business personal property tax. AWS also states it operates 18 solar farms in Virginia generating roughly 2.9 million megawatt hours of clean energy annually, enough by its own estimate to power about 276,000 homes, and that approximately 70 percent of global internet traffic moves through data centers located in the state.

AWS has not published a street address, opening date, floor area, or IT power rating for this individual building, and no county or state economic development record found for this page breaks the Virginia AWS footprint down building by building. What is documented is that this structure sits within the AWS data center footprint the company has confirmed for the Loudoun, Prince William, and Fairfax county corridor, described by the investment, employment, and tax figures above, which report the regional AWS buildout rather than this specific structure.

profile.capacity_note: Not published by AWS at the building level. AWS discloses investment, jobs, and tax totals for its Virginia operations as a whole; it does not report installed or planned IT capacity for individual data center structures.
profile.facility_note: AWS has not identified this specific building by name, function, or construction date in any source found for this page. It is treated here as part of the documented AWS Virginia footprint described above, without an independently confirmed role, tenancy, or expansion status distinct from its campus neighbors.
profile.research_note: Reading written 2026-09-03 by srj-thinpage-writer session (Sonnet). Verified via fresh web search/fetch this session (not reused from 2026-09-02 batch without re-checking): AWS aboutamazon.com investment pages, state/city economic development releases, and named trade/local press, listed in sources. AWS does not publish a per-building street address, opening date, square footage, or IT power rating for this structure; none of the sources checked break the named campus down building by building. profile.regional_context: Northern Virginia is described in trade press as the largest data center market in the world by capacity, anchored by the Loudoun County corridor known as Data Center Alley and now extending into Prince William, Fairfax, and neighboring counties. Alongside AWS, the corridor hosts large campuses operated by Digital Realty, Equinix, Microsoft, Google, Meta, QTS, and CloudHQ, among others. Power for the region comes primarily from Dominion Energy, which has repeatedly identified data center demand as the fastest growing category on its system and has sought new transmission and generation capacity to keep pace. Virginia exempts qualifying data center equipment purchases from state and local sales and use tax under a program administered by the Virginia Economic Development Partnership, an incentive credited by local officials with accelerating the buildout. Local zoning disputes over new campuses, water use for cooling, and Dominion grid capacity have been a recurring subject in Loudoun and Prince William county government since the early 2020s, reported by Virginia Business, Data Center Frontier, and Inside Climate News.

reading.body:
Amazon Web Services does not publish power, capacity, or building-level details for this Northern Virginia data center, so its individual contribution to AI compute cannot be measured from public sources.

The documented numbers describe a region, not a building. AWS reports $51.9 billion in capital and operating expenses on Virginia data center infrastructure from 2011 to 2021, a further $35 billion committed through 2040, $8.2 billion in regional GDP over the same decade, and $334 million in Virginia business personal property tax paid in 2022. The structure sits inside the Loudoun, Prince William, and Fairfax corridor known as Data Center Alley, where AWS has run its US-EAST-1 region since 2006. That region is the company's oldest hyperscale cloud footprint, which makes it a reasonable proxy for how early and how heavily AWS concentrated compute in one power market.

The pattern matters because of where the constraint sits. AWS states that roughly 70 percent of global internet traffic moves through data centers in Virginia, and the corridor is described in trade press as the largest concentration of data centers in the world. Power for the region comes primarily from Dominion Energy, which has identified data center demand as its fastest growing load category and has sought new transmission and generation to keep pace. Virginia's sales tax exemption for qualifying data center equipment is credited by local officials with accelerating the buildout. AWS's own renewable disclosure, 18 solar farms generating about 2.9 million megawatt hours annually, is a supply-side figure for the state, not a statement about this building's load.

What the data does not cover is the building itself. AWS has published no street address, opening date, floor area, or IT power rating for this structure, and no county or state record found here breaks the Virginia footprint down building by building. Of the 326 data center facilities mapped in Virginia, only 23 have published power ratings, totaling 1,375.4 megawatts, and this campus is not among them. The investment, employment, and tax figures are regional totals. They establish that AWS has committed enormous capital to this corridor and that the corridor is the densest concentration of data center capacity in the world, but they cannot tell a reader how much compute this specific building holds or how much of the Dominion grid it draws.
